title: Observation on the means to carry on a war according to Julius Caesar
paragraphs: It is said of many great leaders that they held certain books in special esteem: Alexander the Great, Homer; Scipio Africanus, Xenophon; Marcus Brutus, Polybius; Charles V, Philippe de Commines; and in our day, so they say, Machiavelli still has his following elsewhere. But the late Marshal Strozzi, who had taken Caesar as his man, undoubtedly made the best choice — since Caesar should really be every soldier's breviary, the true and sovereign model of the military art. And, on top of that, God knows with what grace and beauty he has clothed that rich subject, in language so pure, fine, and perfect that, in my opinion, no writings in the world can compare with his on this subject.
I will set down some rare and particular passages from his wars that have stayed in my memory.

When his army was in some panic at the rumour spreading of the great forces King Juba was leading against him, instead of trying to calm his soldiers' fear and play down the enemy's numbers, he called them all together to encourage and reassure them — and took the opposite road from the one we usually take. He told them they need not trouble themselves any further about asking how strong the enemy was, since he was reliably informed of it; and then he named a number that vastly exceeded both the truth and the rumour that was running in his army. He was following Cyrus' advice in Xenophon: it is much less damaging to find an enemy weaker than you expected than to find him really very strong after having been told he was weak.

It was always his practice to train his soldiers simply to obey, without taking it on themselves to pass judgment on, or even talk about, their captain's plans, which he never communicated to them until the very point of execution. He took a pleasure, if they got wind of any of his intentions, in immediately changing his orders to throw them off. For that purpose he would often, after assigning quarters in a place, push on and lengthen his day's march, especially in foul and rainy weather.

When the Swiss, at the start of his wars in Gaul, sent to demand free passage across Roman territory, he was already determined to stop them by force; yet he spoke kindly to their envoys and took some time before answering, in order to use that time to gather his army. Those silly people did not realise what a careful manager he was of his time — for he often repeats that the best part of a captain is to know how to use opportunities, and his speed in his exploits is, in truth, unheard of and incredible.

If he was not very scrupulous about taking advantage of an enemy under cover of a treaty, he was as little scrupulous in another respect: he required no virtue in a soldier but valour, and rarely punished any faults but mutiny and disobedience. He would often, after his victories, turn his men loose to every kind of licence, releasing them for a time from the rules of military discipline — and said that he had soldiers so well trained that, powdered and perfumed, they would still rush furiously to the fight. He liked them to be richly armed, and he gave them engraved, gilt, and damascened armour, so that the care of preserving it would push them to defend it more stubbornly. In speaking to them, he called them "fellow-soldiers," which we still use today; his successor Augustus changed this, supposing Caesar had used the word only out of necessity, and to flatter men who were following him as mere volunteers:
"Rheni mihi Caesar in undis Dux erat; hic socius; facinus quos inquinat, aequat:"
["In the waters of the Rhine Caesar was my general; here at Rome he is my fellow. Crime levels those whom it pollutes." — Lucan, v. 289.]
but this form of address was too low and mean for the dignity of an emperor and general of an army, and so Augustus brought in the custom of simply calling them "soldiers."

With this courtesy Caesar mixed great severity, to keep them in awe. When the ninth legion mutinied near Placentia he discharged them ignominiously, even though Pompey was then still in the field, and only took them back into favour after many entreaties; he quieted them more by authority and boldness than by gentle methods.

Where he speaks of his passage across the Rhine into Germany, he says that he thought it beneath the honour of the Roman people to ferry his army over in boats, and so he built a bridge to let them cross dry-footed. That was the famous bridge he describes in such detail. He never dwells more willingly on his actions than when showing us the ingenuity of his inventions in projects of that sort.

I have noted, too, how much value he set on his exhortations to the soldiers before battle: wherever he wants to show that he was caught off guard or forced into fighting, he always brings in the point that he had no time even to harangue his army. Before that great battle with the people of Tournai: "Caesar," he says, "having given orders for everything else, ran at once where chance led him, to encourage his men; and meeting the tenth legion, had time only to tell them to remember their usual valour, not to be alarmed, and to meet the enemy's onset bravely; and seeing the enemy was already within javelin-range, he gave the signal for battle. Then, going off elsewhere to encourage others, he found they were already engaged." That is what he tells us in that passage. His tongue, in fact, did him notable service on many occasions, and his military eloquence was so highly thought of in his own time that many in his army wrote down his harangues as he spoke them, so that volumes of them were collected that survived long after him. He had so particular a grace in speaking that his close friends — and Augustus among them — could pick out, on hearing the speeches read aloud, even the phrases and words that were not his.

The first time he left Rome on any public command, he reached the Rhone in eight days, with a secretary or two in the coach in front of him constantly writing, and the man carrying his sword behind. And really, even if a man did nothing but travel, he could scarcely match the speed with which Caesar, after being everywhere victorious in Gaul, left it, and, following Pompey to Brundisium, subdued all Italy in eighteen days; returned from Brundisium to Rome; from Rome went into the very heart of Spain, where he overcame extreme difficulties in the war against Afranius and Petreius, and in the long siege of Marseilles; from there he went back into Macedonia, beat the Roman army at Pharsalia, passed in pursuit of Pompey into Egypt, which he also subdued; from Egypt went into Syria and the territories of Pontus, where he fought Pharnaces; from there into Africa, where he defeated Scipio and Juba; returned once again through Italy, where he defeated Pompey's sons:
"Ocyor et coeli fiammis, et tigride foeta."
["Swifter than lightning, or the cub-bearing tigress." — Lucan, v. 405.]

"Ac veluti montis saxum de vertice praeceps Cum ruit avulsum vento, seu turbidus imber Proluit, aut annis solvit sublapsa vetustas, Fertur in abruptum magno mons improbus actu, Exultatque solo, silvas, armenta, virosque, Involvens secum."

["And as a stone torn from the mountain's top by the wind or rain torrents, or loosened by age, falls massive with mighty force, bounds here and there, in its course sweeping from the earth with it woods, herds, and men." — Aeneid, xii. 684.]

Speaking of the siege of Avaricum, he says it was his custom to be with the pioneers night and day. In all enterprises of consequence he reconnoitred in person, and never brought his army into quarters until he had first seen the place; and if we can believe Suetonius, when he resolved to cross into England he was the first man to sound the passage.

He used to say he set more store by a victory won by strategy than by force; and in the war against Petreius and Afranius, when fortune offered him a chance of an obvious advantage, he refused it, saying he hoped, with a little more time but less risk, to overcome his enemies. He also did a notable thing there, ordering his whole army to swim across the river, without any sort of necessity for it:
"Rapuitque ruens in praelia miles, Quod fugiens timuisset, iter; mox uda receptis Membra fovent armis, gelidosque a gurgite, cursu Restituunt artus."

["The soldier rushed through a way to fight which he would have been afraid to take in flight: then, with their armour, they cover wet limbs, and by running restore warmth to their numbed joints." — Lucan, iv. 151.]

I find him a little more temperate and considered in his undertakings than Alexander, who seems to seek out and rush headlong on danger like an impetuous torrent that attacks and crashes against everything it meets, without discrimination or restraint:
"Sic tauriformis volvitur Aufidus; Qui regna Dauni perfluit Appuli, Dum saevit, horrendamque cultis Diluviem meditatur agris;"
["So the bull-shaped Aufidus rolls, which flows through the realm of the Apulian Daunus, when raging, threatens a fearful deluge to the cultivated ground." — Horace, Odes, iv. 14, 25.]

and, indeed, Alexander was a general in the flower and first heat of his youth, whereas Caesar took up the trade at a ripe and well-advanced age. Add to that the fact that Alexander was of a more sanguine, hot, and choleric constitution, which he further inflamed with wine — from which Caesar abstained almost entirely.

But where necessary occasion required, no man ever risked his person more than Caesar did. So much so that, for my part, I seem to read in many of his exploits a settled resolution to throw himself away rather than face the shame of being beaten. In his great battle with the people of Tournai, he charged right up to the head of the enemy without his shield, just as he saw the van of his own army beginning to give ground — and the same thing happened to him several other times. Hearing his people were besieged, he passed through the enemy's army in disguise to encourage them with his presence. Having crossed over to Dyrrachium with very slight forces, and seeing the rest of his army, which he had left to Antony's command, slow to follow him, he set out alone to recross the sea in a tremendous storm, and slipped away in secret to fetch the rest of his troops, with the ports on the other side held by Pompey and the whole sea in his enemy's possession. As for what he accomplished by sheer force of hand, there are many exploits in which the risk goes beyond all the rules of war. With what small means did he undertake to subdue the kingdom of Egypt, and afterwards to attack the forces of Scipio and Juba, ten times greater than his own? These men had I-don't-know-what more-than-human confidence in their fortune; and he used to say that in great undertakings men must embark, not deliberate. After the battle of Pharsalia, when he had sent his army on ahead into Asia and was crossing the Hellespont in a single vessel, he met Lucius Cassius at sea with ten tall warships — and had the courage not only to wait for him but to sail up to him and summon him to surrender, which he did.

When he undertook that furious siege of Alesia, where there were eighty thousand men in garrison, with all Gaul up in arms to raise the siege and a relieving army on foot of one hundred and nine thousand horse and two hundred and forty thousand foot — what boldness and what high confidence it took in him not to give up the attempt but to resolve to face both these enormous difficulties, which he nevertheless overcame; and, after winning that great battle against the army outside, he soon reduced those inside to his mercy. The same thing happened to Lucullus at the siege of Tigranocerta against King Tigranes, but the enemy's quality there was not the same, given the softness of the men Lucullus was dealing with. I will set down here two rare and extraordinary incidents from this siege of Alesia. The first: the Gauls, having mustered their forces against Caesar and made a general review of them, resolved in their council of war to dismiss a good part of that huge multitude, so as not to fall into confusion. This example of fearing to be too many is new; but, properly considered, it stands to reason that the body of an army should be of moderate size and kept within certain bounds, both because of the difficulty of provisioning them and the difficulty of governing them and keeping them in order. At the very least, it is very easy to show by example that monstrously large armies have rarely accomplished anything of substance. As Cyrus says in Xenophon, "It is not the number of men, but the number of good men, that wins the advantage"; the rest only get in the way. And Bayezid based his decision to fight Tamerlane, against the opinion of all his captains, mainly on this — that his enemies' uncountable numbers gave him sure hope of confusion in their ranks. Scanderbeg, a very good and expert judge in such matters, used to say that ten or twelve thousand reliable fighting men were enough for a good leader to keep himself in order in every kind of military situation. The other thing I want to record, which seems contrary to the custom and rules of war, is that Vercingetorix, who was made general of all the parts of the revolted Gaul, went and shut himself up in Alesia. The man who commands a whole country ought never to shut himself up except in such extremity that the only place he has left is in danger, and that his only remaining hope is in the defence of that city; otherwise he should keep himself at liberty, so that he can take general measures for every part of his command.

To return to Caesar. He grew, in time, slower and more considered, as his friend Oppius testifies: thinking he should not lightly hazard the glory of so many victories which one stroke of fortune could take from him. That is what the Italians mean when they want to reproach the rashness and foolhardiness of young people, calling them bisognosi d'onore — "in need of honour" — meaning that, being in such a want and dearth of reputation, they have reason to seek it at any price; which those who have already acquired enough should not do. There may reasonably be some moderation, some satiety, in this thirst and appetite for glory, as in other things; and there are plenty of people who practise it.

He was very far from the religious scruples of the old Romans, who would never prevail in their wars except by sheer pure valour; and yet he was more conscientious than we should be these days, and did not approve of every means to win victory. In the war against Ariovistus, while he was parleying with him, a skirmish broke out among the cavalry, started by the fault of Ariovistus' light horse — and although Caesar saw he had a very great advantage over the enemy at that moment, he would not use it, for fear of being reproached with treacherous dealing.
He always wore rich garments, and of a striking colour, in battle, so as to be more visible and better watched.

He kept a stricter and tighter hand over his soldiers the closer he was to an enemy. When the ancient Greeks wanted to accuse anyone of complete incompetence, they used to say, as a common proverb, that he could neither read nor swim. Caesar was of the same opinion: that swimming was very useful in war, and he himself found it so. When he needed to move fast, he commonly swam across the rivers in his way; he loved to march on foot, as did Alexander the Great. When he was in Egypt and was forced, to save himself, to get into a little boat, and so many men leapt in with him that it was in danger of sinking, he chose rather to trust himself to the sea, and swam to his fleet two hundred paces off, holding his tablets in his left hand and dragging his cloak in his teeth so that it would not fall into the enemy's hands — and at that point in his life he was already fairly far on in years.

Never has any general had such credit with his soldiers. At the start of the civil wars, his centurions offered to find each a man-at-arms at his own expense, and the foot soldiers to serve him at their own cost — and those better off offered, on top of that, to pay for the more necessitous. The late Admiral Chastillon
[Gaspard de Coligny, assassinated in the St Bartholomew massacre, 24 August 1572.]

showed us a similar example in our civil wars; the Frenchmen in his army put up money out of their own purses to pay the foreigners who served with him. Such warm and ready affection among the soldiers of earlier times — who kept strictly to their rules of war — is rarely found in examples; passion has more absolute command over us than reason. And yet it happened, in the war against Hannibal, that following the example of the people of Rome in the city, the soldiers and officers in the army refused their pay, and in Marcellus' camp those who would take any were branded with the name "Mercenaries." Having taken the worst of it near Dyrrachium, Caesar's soldiers came and offered themselves up to be chastised and punished, so that there was more need to comfort than to reprove them. One single cohort of his held off four of Pompey's legions for more than four hours, until they were almost all killed by arrows, so that one hundred and thirty thousand shafts were found in the trenches. A soldier called Scaeva, who held one of the passes, invincibly maintained his position with one eye gone, one shoulder and one thigh shot through, and his shield struck in two hundred and thirty places. It happened that many of his soldiers, when taken prisoner, chose to die rather than promise to go over to the other side. Granius Petronius was taken by Scipio in Africa: Scipio, having put the rest to death, sent him word that he gave him his life, since he was a man of quality and a quaestor. Petronius sent back word that Caesar's soldiers were used to giving others their lives, not to receiving theirs; and immediately killed himself with his own hand.

There are countless examples of their loyalty, but what was done by those besieged in Salona — a city that held out for Caesar against Pompey — must not be forgotten, for the rarity of what happened there. Marcus Octavius was holding them tightly besieged. Inside, they had been reduced to the extreme need of everything: to make up for the lack of men, with most either killed or wounded, they had freed all their slaves; to make ropes for their war-engines they had had to cut off all the women's hair; on top of all this they were starving, and yet they were resolved never to surrender. After the siege had dragged on long enough that Octavius had grown careless and slack in pressing his enterprise, they picked a day about noon, placed the women and children on the walls for show, and sallied out against the besiegers with such fury that they routed the first, second, and third bodies of troops, and then the fourth, and the rest; they beat them clean out of their trenches and chased them right down to their ships. Octavius himself was forced to flee to Dyrrachium, where Pompey lay. I do not at this moment remember another example where the besieged completely defeated the besieger and won the field, or where a sortie produced a pure and total victory.
